activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
knowledge_domain: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
fact: Regular Spanish verbs share the same future endings whether they end in -ar, -er or -ir, so "I will eat" is "comeré" and "I will live" is "viviré."
story:
Eve stared at three charts she had copied from the board, one for verbs ending in -ar, one for -er, one for -ir, and her hand already ached. Ms. Bautista had assigned a paragraph about plans for next year, all in the future tense, due at the end of class. Around her the language room smelled like dry-erase markers and somebody's grape gum, and Lux was drumming his pencil against his desk like a tiny, irritating woodpecker.

"I'm going to fail," Lux whispered. "Three charts. Twenty-something endings. My brain is a tsunami and everything I memorized is underwater."

Eve had written exactly one sentence: El año que viene yo comeré más verduras. Next year I will eat more vegetables, which was a lie, but at least it was a grammatical lie. She flipped back a page in her notebook and found a sentence from yesterday's homework: Yo viviré con mi abuela. I will live with my grandmother. She wrote both verbs side by side and squinted at them.

Comeré. Viviré. One ended in -er and one ended in -ir, but their endings looked the same. That couldn't be right. Teachers loved making things complicated, and Eve had learned the hard way that when something looked easy, it was usually a trap.

She tested it. On a scrap paper she took hablar, an -ar verb, and mashed the -é onto the end the way she had with the other two. Hablaré. Then she checked her chart. Hablaré. Identical. She tried three more, filling the scrap paper with crooked columns, and every single one matched. The three charts on the board were really one chart wearing three costumes.

"Psst. Lux." She slid the scrap paper across the aisle. "Look. Regular verbs share the same future endings whether they end in -ar, -er or -ir. One set. Not three."

Lux stared at it the way people stare at a vending machine that has given them two candy bars. "Then why did I memorize three charts last night?"

"Because we copy what's on the board without looking." Eve grinned, then felt the grin fade a little, because she had lost a whole evening to those charts too, an evening she could have spent at Alyvia's pool.

Alyvia leaned over from the next row, sniffing the paper as if the secret might smell like something. "Show me," she said, and Eve walked her through it once, quietly, while Ms. Bautista helped a boy who had written the same verb four times in a row.

Eve wrote her paragraph fast after that. El año que visitaré a mi abuela en México. Aprenderé a cocinar con ella. Hablaré español todos los días. The words poured out, and for once her pencil kept up with her head. She even added a joke at the end about how she would definitely, honestly eat vegetables, which Alyvia read over her shoulder and snorted at.

At the door, though, Ms. Bautista caught her. "Eve, I saw that scrap paper. Three charts erased, one kept." She held up Eve's notebook. "You crossed out two pages of notes."

"I didn't need them," Eve said, and heard how it came out, half proud and half like she'd thrown away something she'd paid for.

Ms. Bautista handed the notebook back with a small smile. "Keep the crossed-out pages anyway. Sometimes it helps to remember what things cost." Eve slid the notebook into her backpack, the dead charts still faintly visible under the lines of ink, and followed Alyvia out into the hall, where the bell was already ringing.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file, called EXIF metadata.
story:
Jace sat on the floor of Stephanie's living room with her phone balanced on his knee, tapping through the photos she had just sent to the group chat. Stephanie wanted him to help her pick the best shot of the science fair volcano, because the class had been asked to nominate one picture for the school website, and the deadline was tonight. The fake lava had turned out great, orange and blurry with motion, but something else caught his eye before he could choose. When he swiped up on one of the photos Patience had sent from her house, a little map appeared at the bottom of the screen. He leaned closer, smelling the lemon cleaner on Stephanie's floorboards, and saw a red pin sitting on a street he recognized. It was Patience's street, exactly, down to the block.

"Stephanie, come look at this." She crawled over, chewing the last of a granola bar, and frowned at the pin. "Why does your phone know where Patience took her picture?" she asked. Jace tapped the info icon again, and a page of small grey text opened up. It showed numbers, a latitude and longitude, and near the top a label that read EXIF metadata. "That's what it's called," he said slowly. "EXIF metadata." Stephanie read the coordinates out loud like they were a spell.

Jace felt a small, acute worry tighten in his stomach, the same sharp feeling he'd had last summer when his cousin's photo of a scraped knee had somehow shown up on a stranger's account and everyone spent a week arguing about how it spread, like an infection moving through the group chat, one share at a time. "So if Patience sends a picture to the website," he said, "anyone who downloads it could see this? Like, strangers could see exactly where her house is?" Stephanie shrugged, but her thumb had stopped scrolling. "Check one of mine," she said, and pulled up her own volcano photo.

He tapped the same info page on her picture. No pin, no coordinates, just the date and the camera settings. "You must have location off for the camera," he said. He tested it twice more, opening Patience's photo, then Stephanie's, then Patience's again, and the pattern held. Location services on meant the map appeared; off meant nothing. That was the rule, and it was invisible unless you went looking.

Jace texted Patience: turn off location for your camera, then send the volcano again. Two minutes later a new photo arrived, and when he swiped up, the screen showed only the time it was taken. No red pin, no street, no numbers.

"Send this one to the website," Jace said, holding the phone out to Stephanie. She hit send, and the volcano's orange glow lit up the dark screen between them.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: To test whether n is prime, you only need to try divisors up to its square root, because if n is a times b, one of them is no bigger than that root.
story:
Brody leaned closer to Abdul's basement computer, where the desk lamp made a small island of light in the desolate, unfinished corner of the room. Abdul had promised to teach him Python tonight, and the notebook between them held three lines of code: ask for a number, divide it by everything smaller than it, and print "prime" if nothing divided it evenly. It had seemed so simple when Abdul explained it at school. Now Brody watched the cursor blink on a number he had typed in, nine digits long, and the program just sat there, thinking.

"Is it broken?" Brody asked. He pressed a key just to see if the screen would react. It did, so the computer was alive; something inside his program was grinding away. He felt a flicker of dread, the kind he got when a math test had five minutes left and two problems to go. Abdul shrugged and sipped his soda.

Brody stared at the loop in the notebook. For a divisor, it counted from two all the way up to the number itself, one at a time. Millions and millions of trial divisions, all invisible. He began to wonder what the divisions were actually doing. If a number was, say, 6, that was 2 times 3, and if it was 12, that was 3 times 4. Both factors, never both huge. He scribbled on the back page: 2 times 18 is 36, 4 times 9 is 36, 6 times 6 is 36. Every pair he wrote had at least one small number in it. Was that a rule? If a number was a times b, one of them always had to be small, no bigger than the square root of the whole thing. He tested another pair to be sure: 5 times 7 is 35, and 5 is smaller than the square root of 35. The small factor never vanished.

"So I only need to check divisors up to the square root," Brody said slowly. "If nothing up there divides it, nothing above it will either, because one of any pair is always that small." He felt like he had found a hinge and swung a heavy door open with one finger. He changed one line, capping the loop at the square root, saved the file, and typed the nine-digit number again.

The answer flashed onto the screen before he finished letting go of the Enter key: not prime. Brody laughed out loud. "It was fast because the answer was hiding in the small divisors the whole time," he said. "I just made the program search the whole desert when the well was near the house."

Abbul pulled his chair over. "Okay, that was wild. Try it on something with twelve digits."

Brody cracked his knuckles and started typing.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Two-factor authentication asks for a second proof, such as a code sent to your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get into an account.
story:
The envelope had been waiting on the kitchen table that morning, and now the phone sat heavy in Olivia's pocket on the school bus, its screen still showing the setup wizard she hadn't finished. She slid into the seat beside Willow, who peered over immediately.

"Did you integrate your contacts yet?" Willow asked. "Took me forever. Half the numbers in my mom's database came out wrong."

Olivia laughed, but before she could answer, the phone buzzed. A message glowed on the screen: a six-digit code, and above it the words: Your verification code is. She hadn't asked for any code. She hadn't even made an account yet.

"What's that?" Charley leaned over the seat from behind them.

"Nothing," Olivia said, locking the screen. Her stomach had gone tight. A minute later, another buzz. A different code. Then a third.

She remembered something Mr. Gupta had said in the computer club back in September, when he'd helped them set up the club's shared drive. Two-factor authentication, he'd called it, which asks for a second proof, such as a code sent to your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get into an account. At the time she'd thought it was just an extra annoying step. Now she turned it over slowly, staring at the fogged window. Somebody was trying to get into an account. And whoever it was already had her password, because otherwise the codes wouldn't be coming at all. Her password was the school one, the one she'd used everywhere since sixth grade.

"Whoa," Charley said, watching her face. "You look like you saw a ghost."

"Somebody has my password," Olivia said quietly.

Willow's eyes went wide. "Your email?"

The bus rumbled around the corner toward the school. Olivia opened her school account settings, thumbs shaking slightly, and changed the password to something long and new. Then she waited, the phone flat on her palm, watching the screen like a held breath. The bus hissed to a stop. No buzz. No code. She waited through the whole line of kids getting off.

"You're going to miss our stop," Willow said.

"One more second." The screen stayed dark. Whatever had been knocking at her account couldn't get in anymore, not without a second proof, and the second proof came only to her phone, in her hand.

"Ironic," Charley said, climbing over the seat. "The codes that told you something was wrong are the same thing keeping them out."

Olivia stood, dropped the phone into her pocket, and stepped down off the bus into the cold morning air. "New rule," she said. "Different password for everything, starting today."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Honey should not be given to babies under 12 months old, because it can contain bacteria spores that grow in an infant's gut and cause a serious illness called infant botulism.
story:
Anais had babysat exactly zero babies before Saturday, which was why she kept the parents' note in her back pocket and checked it every ten minutes. The baby, Milo, was eight months old, and they were spending the morning at the park by the duck pond because Milo liked watching the ducks and Anais liked having something to look at besides her own nerves. Her little brother's friend Grant had tagged along to feed the ducks, which he claimed was impartial diplomacy between the mallards and the geese, though really he just liked throwing bread.

Milo got fussy around eleven, so Anais settled him in the stroller and dug out the jar of food his mom had packed. Milo refused the spoon, clamping his mouth shut and turning his head like a tiny, determined door slammed shut. Anais thought about it. Babies liked sweet things, everyone knew that. In the pantry at home, her mom kept a squeeze bottle of honey, and Anais remembered she had a packet of honey crackers in her bag from lunch. She reached for the crackers, thinking she could crumble one into the jar and make the food taste better.

"Wait," Grant said, pointing with his bread hand. "Isn't there a note?" Anais pulled the folded paper from her pocket. The parents had written it that morning, and she had only skimmed it.

"Do not give Milo honey," she read. "No honey for babies under 12 months old. It can contain bacteria spores that grow in an infant's gut and cause a serious illness called infant botulism. Not even a little. Not even in crackers." She lowered the note. Her stomach did a slow flip. She had been about to do the exact thing they warned against, and she had walked right up to it without knowing.

"I was going to mix honey into his food," she said. "I was that close." Grant whistled. "So the spores just sit there in honey until a baby digests it, and then, boom?" Anais nodded slowly, then remembered she shouldn't nod like she'd known all along. "Something like that. The note says they grow in his gut." Grant looked at the ducks, then at Milo. "So honey's like a trap that only works on babies. That's the weirdest supervillain origin story ever."

Anais texted her older cousin, who had two kids, to double-check. The reply came fast: "Yep, no honey before their first birthday. Under 12 months, their gut can't handle the spores. After a year it's fine. You did the right thing asking." Anais read it twice, then put the phone away feeling steadier.

The actual problem was still in front of her: Milo was hungry and refusing plain food. She tried warming the jar between her palms first, which her cousin had also suggested in a follow-up message, and then offered the spoon again. Milo considered her with deep suspicion, opened his mouth like a small eager bird, and ate the whole jar. When she burped him, he patted her arm with one fat hand, gently, as if approving her work. Grant fed the last of the bread to an enormous goose and said, "You're basically a professional." Milo burped again, louder this time, and Anais laughed so hard she had to sit down on the bench.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Studies of youth sports have found that players born early in the selection year are picked for teams more often than those born late, which researchers call the relative age effect.
story:
Elizabeth pulled her shin guard out of her locker, and a folded note fell out with it. The locker room smelled like rubber mats and orange peel, and Kaley was already lacing her cleats on the bench beside her. The note was written on a torn corner of the tryout sign-up sheet, in Jiya's loopy handwriting: "Check the birthdays on the posted roster. Count them. Trust me."

"Jiya's being mysterious again," Elizabeth said, waving the note.

"Jiya's always being mysterious. Yesterday she told me my shoelaces were tied in a pattern. They were just tied."

At the wall by the showers, the list of girls who had made the soccer team hung crooked on a pushpin. Elizabeth had missed the cut, and her name was not on it, which was bad enough. But under each name, someone had written the player's birth month for a team-birthday chart the coach was making. She read them off. Sophie, January. Priya, March. Amelia, February. One girl had an October birthday, and one had a November, and then Elizabeth herself, December. She counted twice. Most of the kids who made the team were born early in the year, and the ones born late, like her, mostly had not.

"Maybe the older kids got picked more," she said slowly. "They're not better. They're just months older."

Kaley frowned. "That sounds fake."

"My arm's sore," Jiya announced, bursting in from the hallway and rubbing her shoulder. "Flu vaccine yesterday. Also, I read about your mystery. Kids born early in the selection year get picked for teams way more than kids born late."

"What's that called?" Elizabeth asked.

"The relative age effect," Jiya said, with the smugness of someone who had practiced saying it in the mirror.

Elizabeth exhaled, long and dramatic, and sat down on the bench. Then she stood up again. "Okay. Test. Coach ranked us on speed and skills, but I only got two touches on the ball in the scrimmage because Sophie hogged it. I was hesitant in the drill, sure, but nobody passes to a girl they don't know." She marched to the coach's office door, which had a sign-up sheet taped to it for a second tryout for the practice squad, added that morning.

She wrote her name at the top, then turned around. "Jiya, you're doing my birthday chart next time, and it better say December, in glitter."

"Fine," said Jiya, "but only if you score on Sophie."

Elizabeth grinned and pulled her cleats back on.

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: A bond is a loan from an investor to a government or company, which promises to pay interest and to repay the original amount on a set date.
story:
The sliding doors of Hilltop Grocery exhaled cold air onto Alex's face as he pushed through with the Saturday-morning crowd. In his backpack sat a half-finished sheet for Mr. Hoffmann's class: compare a stock and a bond, say which is riskier and why, due Monday. He had two days, and so far the page held only a doodle of a dollar sign wearing sunglasses.

His mother handed him a list and sent him toward the cereal aisle while she queued for the deli. That was where he ran into Eleonore, who was weighing oranges like they were treasure and reading a battered pamphlet at the same time.

"Don't tell me you finished the Hoffmann thing," Alex said.

"Almost. My grandpa gave me a savings bond years ago, so I asked him about it. Want to hear?" She put an orange back and lowered her voice, as if sharing a secret. "A bond is a loan from an investor to a government or a company. It promises to pay interest and to repay the original amount on a set date."

Alex stared at her. "Wait. A loan? I thought the government loaned you the money."

"No, it's the other way. Grandpa lent the money when he bought the bond. The government borrowed it."

A memory floated up, tranquil and sharp at once: sitting at his grandfather's kitchen table three summers ago, holding a crisp paper bond with his own name on it, feeling rich without understanding what he owned. He had thanked Grandpa, stuck it in a drawer, and never thought about it again. Now he turned the memory over like an orange in his hand. He had been the lender all along. The town, with its roads and library and school, had borrowed from him.

"So a stock," he said slowly, walking with her past the bread racks, "is when you buy a tiny piece of a company, and it can go up or down or vanish. But the bond promises to pay interest and pay back the original amount on a set date."

"Right. Now which is riskier?"

Alex tested it out loud. "Nobody promises you anything with a stock. The company could boom or flop. The bond promises." He paused by the dairy case. "So the stock is riskier. No promise."

"That's what my grandpa said."

At the checkout, Alex's mother was already unloading the cart, and the cashier, who commuted in from two towns over every Saturday, was scanning soup cans at lightning speed. Alex helped bag, still turning the problem over. He remembered Grandpa once saying he wished he'd bought more bonds and fewer stocks before the market dipped years back. Maybe that was wisdom. Maybe it was just a man steadying himself against an old regret. Alex couldn't decide, and Eleonore's shrug in the parking lot said she couldn't either.

Monday felt closer than Monday should. Alex folded the pamphlet Eleonore had lent him, slid it into his bag between the cereal and the milk, and said, "Let's write it tonight."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Nervousness triggers the release of adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach, causing the "butterflies" feeling.
story:
The car smelled like his dad's coffee and the pine air freshener that had died sometime in October. Cameron sat in the back with his tie stuffed in his pocket because wearing it for the whole ride felt like too much commitment. Outside, the gym windows glowed yellow, and he could see shapes moving inside, kids, actual kids, dancing or standing near a wall that the art club had covered in paper stars meant to depict a night sky. His stomach flipped so hard he pressed a hand against it.

"Motion sickness?" his dad asked, glancing in the mirror.

"No. My heart's going fast too, like I ran a mile, but I've been sitting still the whole time." He checked his pulse with two fingers, the way Patience had shown him in science class when they were being meticulous about counting heartbeats per minute. Fast. Really fast, for a person doing nothing but holding a tie.

His phone buzzed. Leonard: "im by the door dont leave me hanging."

Cameron stared at the message and thought it through. His heart was racing and his stomach felt hollow, the feeling everybody called butterflies, even though nothing was flying around in there. When he ran laps in gym, his heart raced like this, but his stomach never felt like this. So the running wasn't what caused the flip. What was different right now? He wasn't moving. He wasn't sick. The only thing happening was that he was nervous, badly nervous, about walking through those doors. So the nervousness itself had to be doing something to his body. Somehow his fear was making his heart speed up and pulling things around inside his stomach. That was strange, but it also meant the feeling wasn't a warning that something was wrong with him. It was just his body reacting to the nerves.

He tried a test. He closed his eyes and pictured himself already inside, already standing next to Leonard, already holding a cup of punch. Nothing bad happened in the picture. His stomach still flipped, but a little less, like the phenomenon was losing its grip the moment he stopped imagining disaster.

"Two minutes," his dad said, pulling into the drop-off line.

Cameron put on the tie, crooked, and fixed it in the window's reflection. He texted back, "coming." His heart was still fast, but he decided that was okay. It could race all it wanted; he was going in anyway. He pushed open the door, and Leonard's voice carried across the parking lot.

"Dude, you made it. The DJ just played a whole song about tacos. You missed everything."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: Repeating an experiment several times and averaging the results reduces the effect of random errors in any single trial.
story:
Matthew measured the distance from the catapult to where the tennis ball landed, wrote down 9.4 meters, and frowned. Layla, who had come over to test her own catapult for the science fair, leaned over his shoulder.

"Nine meters? Mine only went six." She set her machine on the grass beside his, a plank and a spoon lashed together with rubber bands, and pulled the arm back. The ball sailed over the fence and into the neighbor's tomato plants. "Okay, that one was way too far," she said. "The last one barely cleared the picnic table."

Memphis, sprawled on the porch steps eating leftover Thai cuisine from a takeout box, pointed his fork at her. "So which one is your real distance, six meters or the tomato launch?"

"That's the problem. I don't know. The wind isn't even the same from one throw to the next. Something random happens each time." Layla stared at the tomato plants, then at Matthew. "You're the one who reads about scientists. How do they handle this?"

Matthew thought about it. He remembered that before every rocket launch he'd watched online, the team ran test after test, day after day, and only then announced a number. Maybe the tests weren't for show. "Try it again," he said. "Not once. Like ten times, and we'll write every result down."

Layla reloaded. The ten launches were messy, unpredictable things. One went sideways. One landed with a bounce that made Memphis laugh so hard he dropped his fork. But when Matthew added the ten distances together on his notepad and divided, the number came out steady, close to six and a half meters, with no wild jumps. The tomato launch, it turned out, was the strange one, an outlier hiding among ordinary throws. "One crazy launch doesn't matter when you do all ten and average them," Matthew said. "One random error gets smaller when it's only one out of ten."

The day of the fair, Ms. Francis walked the aisle of gymnasium tables. She paused at Layla's project, saw the chart of ten trials and the average, and nodded. Then she stopped at the next table, where a boy stood beside a gleaming catapult with a single number written large on his poster: 12 meters. He launched once for her, and the ball dribbled out sideways and rolled to a stop at two meters.

"The trials that precede your demonstration should agree with it," Ms. Francis said mildly, and moved on.

Layla caught Matthew's eye across the aisle. "One out of ten," she whispered, and held up her chart. "I got lucky nine more times than he did."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: Simple interest is paid only on the original amount deposited, called the principal, so it adds the same dollar amount every year.
story:
Nicolas had earned forty dollars running the lemonade stand all summer, and today he was going to open his first savings account. He spread the money on the card table next to the pitcher, all crumpled ones and a few fives, and counted it twice while Paislee squeezed lemons behind him.

"Forty dollars and two quarters," he said. "The bank lady said I'd earn interest."

Paislee wrinkled her nose. "What kind of interest?"

"I don't know. There were two kinds on the brochure." He had taken the brochure home and read it on the porch, which was tranquil in the late afternoon except for Angus drumming his fingers on the railing. The brochure said one kind was simple and one was compound. It hadn't said much else that made sense.

The next week, Nicolas went back to the bank with his grandfather and got a statement. He laid it out on the lemonade table where Angus and Paislee could see it. "Look. First year, I deposited forty dollars. Interest paid: two dollars." He pointed at the second line. "Second year, two dollars again. Exactly the same."

"That's boring," Angus said. "It should grow."

"That's what I thought too." Nicolas flipped the brochure over. "But see, this kind is called simple. Simple interest is paid only on the original amount you deposited, the principal. So it just adds the same dollar amount every year. Two dollars, then two dollars, then two dollars."

Paislee tapped the corner of the brochure. "And the other kind? The compound one?"

"I haven't figured that out yet. The statement only shows the simple account." He tried to categorize what he knew: same amount every year meant simple, and if the amount ever changed, it must mean something else. But he wanted proof. So he made a deal with his grandfather. If Nicolas kept the lemonade stand going every Saturday for the rest of the summer, his grandfather would switch the account to the compound kind, whatever that did.

Angus, who had been certain all along that banks were "basically a scam," studied the statement for a long moment. "Okay," he admitted. "It's not a scam. It's just slow."

"It's slow like a lemon tree," Paislee said, and she hung a new sign on the stand that said LEMONADE: SWEET NOW, SWEETER LATER. Angus called it propaganda for lemons, but he helped her tape it up anyway.

In September, Nicolas set the new statement beside the old one. The interest line was not two dollars anymore. It was more, and he grinned so wide he had to set down the pitcher.

"Next summer," he told Paislee, "we sell in front of the soccer fields."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift after spellings had started to become fixed, which is a major reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation.
story:
The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and nervous sweat, and Aiden's word was next on the list. He had missed "bite" three times in practice this week, adding an extra t, dropping the e, once writing "bight" because that was the only way the letters made sense to him. Now the district spelling bee, the prestigious one with the trophy in the glass case by the front office, came down to him, Amelya, and a kid from another school.

"Contestant fourteen, your word is 'mice.'"

Mice. Short i, but it was spelled like "nice," which had a long i, which made no sense at all. Aiden closed his eyes. Earlier that week he'd stormed into the library and complained to Amelya that English spelling was broken, and she had slid a book across the table.

"It's called the Great Vowel Shift," she'd said, tapping the page. "Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed after spellings had started to become fixed."

"So the letters stayed put," Aiden had said slowly, "and the sounds moved out from under them."

"Exactly. That's a big reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation."

Viola had leaned over from the next seat. "So every weird silent e is basically a fossil." She'd grinned. "You could thrive on this. Patterns everywhere."

The consequence of skipping the library that day, Aiden now understood, would have been a very short bee. But he hadn't skipped it, and he'd spent two evenings testing his idea. Words with the old long vowels, the ones that shifted, kept their shifting-prone spellings: "find," "child," "wide." Words that never had those vowels, like "mitten" and "sick," stayed honest. He'd made a list, said them aloud, and the pattern held almost every time.

"Mice," he said. "M-I-C-E." Then he added, before he could stop himself, "It follows the pattern from the Great Vowel Shift. The i would have said one thing in 1400 and says another now."

A ripple of laughter went through the bleachers. Ms. Nair, running the microphone, gave him a small nod that meant she knew exactly what he was talking about, and said, "That is correct."

Amelya got "chief" and spelled it wrong, hooking her shoulders forward when the bell rang. Viola survived "dream," "throat," and then stumbled on "geese," throwing an extra e in front of the s. The kid from the other school went down on "breakfast."

"Aiden, your final word is 'wise.'"

He pictured his list. Old long i, the kind that had shifted, one that would have rhymed differently centuries ago. He knew this word's whole family: wide, ice, drive, bite, the fossil e riding silently at the end of every one of them.

"W-I-S-E. Wise."

"We have a winner," Ms. Nair said, and somewhere behind him, Viola cupped her hands and yelled, "Fossil power!"

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Chinese culture, a clock is usually avoided as a gift, because the phrase 'giving a clock' sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death.
story:
Louis stood in the school hallway with ten minutes before the bell, staring at the flyer Tiffany had taped to her locker. The Chen family had just moved into the house next door to his, and his mom had asked him to pick a small housewarming gift on his way home from school. In his backpack, wrapped in newspaper, sat a clock. A good one, too, with a cherrywood frame and a soft tick he could hear right through the paper.

"It's for the new neighbours," he told Tiffany and Summer at lunch, sliding the package halfway across the table so they could hear the ticking. He kept his hands folded like they taught him at his grandmother's, elbows off the table, and waited for someone to say nice choice.

Summer went pale. "Wait, the Chens? You know they're Chinese, right? You can't give them a clock. In Chinese culture a clock is usually avoided as a gift, because 'giving a clock' sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death."

"You're making that up," Louis said, though his stomach dropped. He tried to build an inference from what he knew: Summer studied Mandarin on weekends and had once corrected his pronunciation of "dumpling" in front of everyone. She was wrong about a lot of things, like the time she insisted the gym had a second floor. But she was never wrong about language stuff. Never once, that he could remember.

"It's true," Tiffany said quietly. "My aunt married into a Chinese family and she told me the same thing. Ask the Chens yourself if you don't believe us." Commuting to school with a doomed clock suddenly seemed like the worst part of Louis's day, and it was a forty-minute trip.

After last period he stopped by Ms. Reyes's room anyway, just to check, and she only shrugged and said Summer would know better than she did. That settled it. On the walk home Louis ducked into the corner shop and used his allowance on a tin of jasmine tea and a box of tangerines, which the cashier said people brought when someone moved. At the Chens' door, he knocked twice, waited, and held out the bag with both hands like his mom had drilled into him since he was little, because in his house one-handed anything was rude.

Mrs. Chen opened the door, looked into the bag, and smiled wide enough to crinkle her eyes. "Tangerines," she said. "Good luck. And tea for the whole housewarming. You come in, we're just sitting down to eat." Behind her, Louis could see steam rising from a table crowded with dishes, and the clock stayed home in his closet, ticking away at nothing.

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
knowledge_domain: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
fact: Masking fluid is a liquid rubber painted onto areas to keep them white; once it dries you paint over it, then rub it off to reveal the paper.
story:
Mia stared at the paint swatch taped above her easel and felt like she was standing at the edge of a lake with no rudder. Ms. Chen had said portraits in watercolour were built like sandcastles from the sky down: a pale wash first, then darker ones, layer after layer. But where would the white of Chelsey's necklace go, the tiny bright dots that made the beads look round, if every layer of paint covered the whole paper? She speculated that maybe you just painted around them with a needle-thin brush, but her hand trembled when she imagined steering around forty beads the size of sesame seeds.

"That necklace is going to vanish under the dark shirt," said Mohammad, leaning over from the next easel. His portrait of his cat already had three layers of grey and looked mysteriously wise, like a judge.

"I know," Mia groaned. "It's like trying to keep snow white while painting a mud puddle over it."

She flipped through the supply drawer for the fourth time, hunting for magic, and found a small amber bottle with a lid crusted like honey. The label had half worn away, but she could read the words MASKING FLUID. She shook it, sniffed it, and made a face. "Smells like a rubber duck's nightmare."

Chelsey, who was supposed to be painting and was actually braiding and unbraiding the same strand of hair, drifted over. "What's masking fluid?" she asked.

"You paint it on, and it keeps the paper white," Mia said slowly, reading the back of the bottle. "It dries, you paint right over it, then you rub it off and the white comes back, like a ghost leaving a room."

"A ghost that does your homework," Mohammad said. "Best ghost ever."

Mia tested it on a scrap first, because a good sailor checks her rudder before the storm. She dabbed the milky liquid into little dots, waited until they dried tacky, brushed a sweep of dark blue across the whole scrap, then rubbed at one dot with her fingertip. It balled up like eraser crumbs and rolled away, and underneath sat a perfect white circle, glowing against the blue like a porthole into another, brighter room. Her whole chest did a somersault.

She dotted the fluid onto every bead in Chelsey's necklace, plus a tiny spark on the locket, then let it dry while she mixed the shirt colour, a deep green-blue she privately called dragon pool. She painted the whole collar in three fearless strokes, right over the dots, and it felt illegal, wonderful, like walking through walls.

When the layer dried, she rubbed each bead with a clean finger. The rubber crumbled away and the necklace appeared bead by bead, as if an invisible jeweller were stringing it for her out of light. Mohammad leaned in so far he almost put his elbow in his water cup, and Ms. Chen paused behind them, said nothing, and smiled at the paper.

"Chelsey, your necklace," Mia said, holding it up. "Ghost-delivered."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: The 2019 Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right.
story:
Addison sat at the kitchen table with her laptop open, the living room behind her already humid from the kettle her dad had left boiling. Tonight was the school spelling bee, and because the gym floor was being refinished, the whole thing was happening online, spellers at home, one camera each. Her dad kept generating nervous little errands, wiping the counter, refilling her water, until she finally said, "Dad, I can spell better when you're not doing that."

The problem wasn't the camera. The problem was Clarissa. Clarissa had won the school bee three years running; she was a veteran of the regional round too, and last week she had told everyone in the cafeteria that this year's trophy was already hers. Addison had come second to her twice, and second felt like a word with a letter missing. She wanted the win, and she knew exactly who stood in the way.

Round one went smoothly. Round two, Alisa went out on "rhubarb," her face crumpling before her microphone even cut off. Round by round the list shrank until only Addison and Clarissa were left, and Ms. Ma, judging from a split screen of ten squares, kept reading harder words. Addison got "chrysanthemum." Clarissa got "appoggiatura" and spelled it without blinking. Addison got "perspicacious." Clarissa got "mnemonic." Neither of them missed.

That was when Addison remembered something she'd read in the article her mom had printed out for her, the one she'd used to generate a practice list last month. In 2019, the Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right. Eight winners. Sharing the title. Nobody lost. Addison had skipped past that part at the time, but now, three rounds past the scheduled ending with her heart hammering and Clarissa looking just as tired in her little square, it came back to her. The words didn't have to keep going until somebody cracked. The words could simply run out.

Ms. Ma looked at her own list, then into the camera. "I have one word left," she said. "If both of you spell it, you'll be co-champions. If one of you misses it, the other wins outright."

Addison glanced at the trophy shelf behind Clarissa's shoulder, the three shiny cups already there, waiting for company. Clarissa caught her looking and gave a small, strange half-smile.

"Ready?" Ms. Ma asked.

"Ready," they said at the same time, and Ms. Ma opened her mouth to read the last word.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the atomic number also tells you how many electrons it has.
story:
Willem's model of a sodium atom was beautiful, and it was wrong, and he had fifteen minutes before the judge reached their table.

"You gave it nine electrons," Andrew said, counting the little foam balls on wire rings for the third time, as if they might multiply if he stared hard enough. "Sodium has eleven."

"It has as many as it wants," Willem said, hot-gluing a proton to the nucleus. "It's my atom."

Andrew dragged the laminated periodic table across the table, the one Ms. Korhonen had lent them after deciding the fair's copy belonged in the "reference" category rather than the "decoration" category. His finger found Na in the third row, then slid up to the number printed above the symbol. "Eleven. That's the atomic number. That's how many protons you glued in there."

"So?"

"So it's neutral," Andrew said. "No charge. Which means the electrons have to balance it out. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. Eleven and eleven."

Willem looked at his model the way you look at a dog that has done something on the carpet. "Nobody can see electrons anyway. I could exclude them entirely and call it a minimalist art piece."

"You cannot exclude electrons from an atom. That's like excluding the cheese from a pizza and still calling it pizza."

Maelys appeared from behind the neighboring display, a poster about whether cafeteria smoothies are actually nutritious, which according to her data were mostly sugar wearing a fruit costume. She held out her palm. "Give me nine foam balls and a hot glue gun, and nobody gets embarrassed in front of Ms. Korhonen."

The wire rings on the model had spaces for two electrons in the inner ring, eight in the middle, and one lonely ball on the outer ring, which was the whole reason Andrew had started counting in the first place. One ball alone on the outside. It looked like the atom was raising its hand to ask a question. He had thought about that electron for two days before understanding why it mattered, and now he watched Maelys snap the last one into place just as Ms. Korhonen's shoes stopped in front of their table.

"Tell me about your element," she said.

"Sodium," Willem said, with the confidence of a boy whose model now contained the correct number of everything. "Eleven protons, and since it's neutral, eleven electrons too. The atomic number tells you both."

Ms. Korhonen raised one eyebrow, then wrote something on her clipboard. "And what is that lone electron doing way out there?"

Willem looked at Andrew. Andrew looked at Willem. Maelys whispered, "Say it's raising its hand."

"It's the weird one, ma'am," Willem said. "It doesn't want to sit with the others."

"Neither does sodium," she said, and moved on to the smoothies.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: The phone Martin Cooper used for the first handheld cell phone call weighed about 1.1 kilograms (2.5 pounds).
story:
Ms. Lavoie set a cardboard box on the lab table and said, "Before anyone gets excited, this is not a quiz. It's show and tell, and it's mine."

She held up an ancient brick of a phone, grey and scuffed, with a rubber antenna sticking out the top like a crooked finger. "This belonged to my father. He carried it around like a dumbbell."

Luke raised his hand. "How much does it weigh?"

"A little over a kilogram," she said. "About two and a half pounds. The phone Martin Cooper used for the first handheld cell phone call weighed about that much, and this thing is nearly its twin."

Aarav snorted. "Two and a half pounds? My phone weighs less than my math homework."

"My phone weighs less than my sandwich," said Jacob, "and I checked."

Luke pulled out his own phone, the one he'd gotten three days ago, and it disappeared into his palm like a playing card. He set it on the scale they used for chemistry. One hundred and sixty grams. He did the subtraction twice in his head. The old phone was more than six times heavier. His grandfather had laughed at dinner on Sunday, saying phones used to be for building muscles, but Luke hadn't believed him until now.

"Okay," he said slowly, "so here's my theory. If that thing weighed two and a half pounds, nobody carried it for fun. They carried it because they had to. So people only used phones when it mattered." He held up his own phone. "Mine weighs nothing, so I use it for everything. That's the hidden cost. The lighter it gets, the more I use it."

"Sinister," said Jacob. "Your phone is secretly plotting against you."

"My phone IS me," Luke said. "That's the problem."

Ms. Lavoie leaned against her desk. "And what do you anticipate doing about this sinister plot?"

Luke thought for a second. "A test. I'm going to carry something heavy. Like a small weight in my pocket, one kilogram, one point one to match the original. Every time I pull out my phone, I hold the weight first. If it's not worth holding the weight, it's not worth unlocking the screen."

"That's the weirdest phone plan I've ever heard," said Aarav.

"It's heritage," Luke said. "Respecting the ancestors. They suffered so I could scroll."

Aarav rummaged in the supply cabinet and came back with a iron mass from the physics shelf, stamped 1.1 kg. He dropped it into Luke's palm with a thud.

Luke pocketed it, felt the honest drag against his hip, and slid his phone into the same pocket beside it.

"First scroll of the new era," he announced, and reached past the phone for the weight.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: The independent variable is the one thing a scientist changes on purpose, and the dependent variable is what gets measured to see the effect.
story:
Charles lined up six paper airplanes on the black lab table, each one a little different from the last. One had wide wings, one had narrow wings, one had a bent nose, and three others he had folded at midnight because he could not sleep. The science fair was in two days, and his data sheet was a mess.

"You changed everything," said Anis, squinting at his notes. "Wide wings, heavy paper, pointy nose. How do you know which thing made the difference?" Jax picked up the wide-winged plane and tossed it across the room, where it smacked into the window above the sink. Mr. Sutton looked up from his desk but said nothing.

Charles stared at the scribbled numbers on his sheet. Last year flashed back to him, the fourth-grade fair when his volcano had won nothing because the judge kept asking what he had actually tested. He had not known then. He had just mixed things until foam went everywhere and it looked cool. He was twelve now, and he did not want that feeling again.

"Okay," he said slowly, picking up the plane Jax had thrown. "I have to change only one thing on purpose. That's the thing I'm testing." Anis nodded. "My sister called that the independent variable. The independent variable is the one thing a scientist changes on purpose, and the dependent variable is what gets measured to see the effect." Charles wrote the words at the top of a fresh data sheet, then underlined them.

"So what's your one thing?" Jax asked, dragging three chairs out of the way to clear a runway. Charles sorted the planes, trying to classify them into groups by wing shape alone, but his folds were too sloppy and the piles overlapped. He decided to start over with plain printer paper, same weight, same size, changing nothing but the width of the wings.

He folded four new planes while Anis measured wing spans with a ruler and Jax marked a starting line on the floor with tape. The first plane, narrow wings, sailed past the second lab station. Charles paced off the distance and wrote it down, then glanced at a shelf where a porous chalk eraser sat next to a cup of cracked pencils. One pencil had a hairline fracture running down its yellow paint, and it made him think of his old volcano project, split open and useless. Not this time.

He launched the second plane, and it glided straight toward the window where the wide-winged one still lay. "Seventeen steps!" Anis called out, pencil scratching across the data sheet.

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: The Scottish geologist James Hutton argued in 1785 that slow, everyday processes like erosion, working over immense time, shaped Earth's surface.
story:
The planetarium's basement exhibit hall was humid from the sprinklers outside, and Anais pressed her notebook against her chest so Kathryn couldn't read the half-empty page. Mr. Mori had assigned each of them one station on the geology floor, and hers was the canyon table: a long tray of packed sand with a pump that pushed a thin ribbon of water from one end to the other. In two minutes, she was supposed to explain to the whole class how a river the size of a garden hose could ever carve something like the Grand Canyon.

"I look like a total fraud standing here," Anais muttered. Kathryn was already across the room at the glacier station, grinning at her own chunk of blue gelatin. Finlay wandered over, chewing a granola bar.

"A stream table," Finlay said. "My cousin in the science club had one. You could run it all day and it still wouldn't make a canyon."

"That's exactly my problem." Anais turned the pump on and watched the water braid itself through the sand, carrying grains downstream and dropping them in a little fan where the slope flattened. "It moves stuff, sure. But canyons are huge. This is nothing."

Kathryn hurried over holding a folded note she'd scribbled at the glacier station and slid it across the table. It read: "There's a quote painted above the door on your way in. I think it's meant for you. Signed, a friend who charges no fees." Anais looked up at the archway behind them, and there it was, in small gold letters: slow, everyday processes like erosion, working over immense time, shaped Earth's surface, argued by the Scottish geologist James Hutton in 1785.

Anais read it twice. "1785," she said slowly. "So he wasn't talking about running a pump for an afternoon. He meant the water just keeps going. Years beyond counting." She crouched and nudged the pump to its lowest setting, so the water ran barely faster than a trickle. "Finlay, we'll leave it like this while we eat lunch. If it still moves sand at the weakest flow, then strength isn't the point. Time is."

After lunch they found a shallow trench, nothing grand, but unmistakably deeper, with a small ridge of deposited sand built up at its mouth where the water had dropped what it carried. Finlay got his phone out to take a picture. When Mr. Mori called the class to gather, Anais stood beside the table, opened her notebook, and pointed at the groove in the sand.

"James Hutton," she said, "figured this out with no stream table at all."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: A small amount of stress before a test or a game can sharpen focus; stress becomes harmful mainly when it lasts for a long time without relief.
story:
Piper sat cross-legged on her grandmother's porch steps, staring at the pool behind the house where her grandfather swam laps every morning, slow and even, like a metronome. On Saturday she would race the two-hundred freestyle for the first time, and her stomach had been knotting itself for days. She had come to her grandparents' house for the week, partly to train in the quiet pool, and partly because at home she could not stop chewing the inside of her cheek.

Her grandmother set down two glasses of lemonade and studied her. "You've been waking at three in the morning. I hear you pacing." Piper hadn't known anyone could hear her. She admitted it, and also the tight shoulders, the snap she'd taken at Rafael for borrowing her goggles, the way her thoughts spun when she lay in the dark. Her grandmother didn't lecture. She just said, "Tonight, screens off an hour before bed, same time every night, and I'll show you something my swim coach taught me in 1968." On the porch, she walked Piper through slow breathing: in for four counts, out for six, shoulders dropping on the exhale. Piper practiced until the hummingbirds stopped blurring in front of her eyes.

That night, keeping the routine, she lay in the dark and her mind drifted to Krystal, who had quit the relay team two weeks ago. Everyone assumed Krystal was just tired of losing. But Piper kept turning over the details: Krystal had stopped eating lunch, stopped laughing at Rafael's terrible similes about the coach's whistle, and had said, once, that she felt like she was carrying sand in her chest. That wasn't the same as Piper's race jitters, which came and went like weather. Krystal's heaviness had lasted for weeks, without a break. Piper sat up in bed, suddenly sure. A little stress before a race could sharpen you; her grandmother had even said so, that hers had made her faster. But stress that stayed that long, that never let go, was a different thing altogether.

At breakfast, Piper texted Krystal: "Can you come over? My grandma makes cinnamon toast." The three dots appeared, vanished, appeared again. Finally: "ok."

Krystal arrived with her hair unbrushed and her swimsuit still in her bag, as if she'd meant to pack it and couldn't finish. They sat on the porch steps, and Piper let the silence stretch while a lawnmower droned somewhere down the street. She could feel the thing Krystal wasn't saying sitting between them like a third glass of lemonade. Piper cherished this friendship, the years of shared lanes and burnt summer pancakes, and she wasn't going to lose it to guessing.

"You don't have to race Saturday," Piper said finally. "But I don't think you've just been tired. I think it's been bad for a long time, and I think you should talk to Ms. Papadopoulos. She listens." Krystal looked at the pool, where the morning light lay flat and silver on the water. Her breath went in, four counts, and out, six, the way Piper had shown her without either of them naming it.

"Okay," Krystal said. "Monday. But you owe me cinnamon toast."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In a 1974 study by Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, people who were asked how fast cars 'smashed' into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked about cars that 'hit.'
story:
The community centre gym smelled like popcorn and floor wax, because rehearsal for the spring play shared the space with a birthday party two rooms over. Jayden was hauling a folded table toward the storage closet when it happened: Jayce came around the corner fast, Trent came the other way faster, and the two of them collided so hard that Trent's water bottle spun across the synthetic floor and slapped against the wall. Jayden saw the whole thing. Mostly.

Ten minutes later, Ms. Dlamini arrived with her clipboard, and Jayden watched something odd begin. She asked Trent first, "How fast were you going when you smashed into him?" Trent rubbed his shoulder and said, "Pretty fast. Maybe running speed." Then she turned to Jayce, who had been standing still, and asked, "How fast was he going when he hit you?" Jayce squinted and said, "Not that fast, actually. He sort of clipped me." Same crash. Two very different answers. Ms. Dlamini's pen paused above the clipboard, and Jayden felt his brain start to itch.

He had been trying to condense his notes from a psychology video he'd watched for science class into one page of index cards, and one card floated up in his memory now. He dug the card out of his backpack and found the line he wanted: in a 1974 study by Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, people who were asked how fast cars smashed into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked how fast the cars hit. Jayce leaned over his shoulder. "Oh, the Loftus and Palmer thing," Jayce said. "We watched that too. The smashed people said faster speeds than the hit people. Same video."

"So it's not that Trent lied," Jayden said slowly. "It's that the question changed the answer." He wanted to check, not just assume. So when Ms. Dlamini came back with ice for Trent's shoulder, Jayden asked her, "Can I try something? Ms. Dlamini, how fast would you say Jayce was going when he collided with Trent?" She considered it. "Moderate, I'd say. A quick walk." Then he asked Trent, "How fast was Jayce going when he smashed into you?" Trent didn't even hesitate. "Fast. He came out of nowhere."

Jayce burst out laughing, and even Trent grinned around his ice pack. "So I'm the monster now?" Trent said. Ms. Dlamini wrote something on her clipboard, then flipped it around so they could see: witness statement unreliable, check wording of questions. "Thank you, Jayden. You may have just saved us from blaming the wrong person." Jayden slid his index card back into his bag and said, "Ask Jayce's version one more time. I want to hear if the adaptation of my experiment works on him too."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: The method of loci is a memory trick of linking each part of a text to a place along a familiar route, then walking that route in your mind to recall it.
story:
Muhammad stood at the gate of the cemetery holding a folded paper with the prayer printed on it, and he had memorized exactly one line in three days. His ceremony was on Saturday. It was Wednesday.

"Walk with me," said Monroe, who had come along because his grandmother was buried here and he visited every week anyway. "Fresh air helps your brain. That's a scientific probability. Probably."

They strolled past the old stone wall, past the oak with the crooked bench beneath it, past the little gate to the new section. Muhammad read the prayer aloud for the tenth time, and the words slid off him like rain off a waxed jacket. "It's no use. Some kids thrive at this. I am not one of them."

Monroe stopped by the bench. "Say the first line here."

"What?"

"Just do it."

Muhammad said the first line. Then Monroe pointed at the oak. "Second line goes there. The little gate gets the third." By the time they had walked the whole route, each line of the prayer had a place, and when Muhammad walked back and looked at the wall, the bench, the oak, the gate, and the rest, the lines came up out of the ground like spring bulbs. He said the whole prayer without the paper, and he shouted so loudly that a rabbit bolted from the grass and Monroe fell over laughing.

"There's a name for that," Muhammad said that afternoon, after he had looked it up. "The method of loci. You link each part of a text to a place along a familiar route, then walk that route in your mind to recall it."

On Friday he practiced the whole walk in his head, eyes closed, three times. But on Saturday morning his mother drove him to the ceremony and his mind went suddenly, horribly blank. He stood up in front of everyone feeling as vulnerable as a snail without its shell. The wall. Nothing. The bench. Nothing. He panicked. Then he remembered that he did not have to picture this cemetery. The route could be anywhere familiar, so he walked, in his mind, through his grandmother's house: front door, hallway, the kitchen with the singing kettle, her room with the blue quilt. Each line sat in a room, waiting for him like a cat on a chair. He recited the prayer straight through, every line, and sat down to the loudest clapping he had ever caused.

Afterward, Mr. Malik, who led the ceremony, shook his hand and said, "Most boys repeat it like a recorded message. You said it like you were walking somewhere."

"I was," said Muhammad. "Kitchen, kettle, blue quilt."

Mr. Malik looked a little worried, but Muhammad just grinned and waved the folded paper, still in his pocket, never opened, over his head like a flag.

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: The Galápagos finches have beaks suited to different foods, such as thin beaks for picking insects and deep, heavy beaks for cracking hard seeds.
story:
Noah stood at the kitchen table with a shoebox of junk he had collected from the back of the pantry: tweezers, a nutcracker, a spoon, and a pair of pliers. Ms. Sharma had assigned a project on the finches of the Galápagos Islands, and tomorrow each student had to explain, in front of the class, how natural selection could change the shape of a bird's beak. Noah had read the chapter twice and still felt like he was reciting words he didn't own yet.

Last semester he had made the opposite choice. He had memorized a paragraph about photosynthesis, delivered it flat, and watched Micaela's volcano foam over the desk while the whole class leaned forward. He had told himself that memorizing was safer, but standing there while everyone looked at the volcano, he wasn't so sure. This time he wanted something people could see.

So he had called Jia, who was already halfway up the driveway with a bag of sunflower seeds and a jar of dried mealworms from the pet store. "Ms. Sharma said to be convincing," Jia said, dumping the seeds into a pile. "She likes it when you emphasize the evidence, not just the conclusion."

They set up the table like the islands themselves. One corner was the wet, insect-heavy island, with the mealworms scattered under a layer of paper strips. The other corner was the dry island, where Jia had glued sunflower seeds into a block so they couldn't be picked up, only cracked. Noah scattered paper clips as "seeds" on a third pile, and small rubber bands as insects on a fourth, until the whole table was a map of different islands.

"You be the bird," Noah said, handing her the tweezers. Jia went to the insect island first and picked out the rubber bands one by one, quick and clean. Then she tried the tweezers on the glued seeds. She squeezed until her hand cramped, and the seed sat there whole. She could not crack it. "Switch," Noah said, and gave her the nutcracker. On the seed block she split the hull of a sunflower seed on the first try and cracked three more in a row. But when she took the nutcracker to the insect island, she knocked the rubber bands around and caught none of them.

Noah wrote the results in his notebook and stared at them. The thin tool caught insects and failed on seeds. The heavy tool cracked seeds and failed on insects. He flipped back through what he'd read and checked it against the table. The birds with thin beaks picked insects, and the birds with deep, heavy beaks cracked hard seeds. That was consistent with everything in front of him. "So on the insect island," he said slowly, "the birds with thin beaks get more food, more of them survive, and over time that's all there is. That's the whole thing. That's natural selection."

"You changed your mind," Jia said. "Yesterday you told me this project was boring."

"It was boring when it was just a page in a book." Noah picked up the tweezers, walked to the seed block, and squeezed them against a sunflower seed one last time. The seed didn't even crack.

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Most traditional bar soaps are basic, with a pH of around 9 to 10.
story:
The litmus paper had been sitting in Brooklyn's backpack since Tuesday, when Mr. Thompson handed out strips to anyone who wanted extra practice before the quiz. She had planned to test things at home, but then her mother announced they were spending Saturday at Grandma's, helping clear out the garage. Now, while the grown-ups argued over whether a box of old gardening tools counted as a keep or a giveaway, Brooklyn stood at Grandma's kitchen sink with the little paper strips and a jar of vinegar she had found under the counter.

She had her phone propped against the window, texting Adalynn between tests. "Testing vinegar first," she typed, and dipped a strip in a spoonful of it. The paper flashed from blue to a pink so bright it looked almost defiant against the white saucer. "Acid," she wrote, feeling a small thrill. Something invisible was showing itself, a hidden property she couldn't see or touch but could catch on paper. She had gotten a B minus on the last lab because she'd rushed and mislabeled her samples, and she still remembered the flat feeling of that. This time she was going slowly, one thing at a time.

Grandma wandered in with a dust rag and peered over her shoulder. "What are you doing to my saucer, child?"

"Science homework. I'm testing stuff to see if it's acid or base." Brooklyn held up the pink strip. "Vinegar's an acid. Watch."

She turned on the tap, wet her hands, and pumped the dispenser of soap by the sink until suds ran down over her fingers. Then she caught a drop of the soapy water on a fresh strip of blue litmus paper. Nothing happened. She frowned, dipped it again, and this time the blue deepened, and when she tried a red strip in the same soapy water, it turned blue.

"That's weird," she said out loud. "It went the opposite way from the vinegar."

"What's opposite about it?" Grandma asked.

"Vinegar turned blue paper red, and soap turned red paper blue. They're opposites on the scale." Brooklyn wiped her hands and pulled out her phone to check the chart Mr. Thompson had printed. Most traditional bar soaps were basic, with a pH of around 9 to 10. Her strip, compared against the chart's colors, sat right there, near the top of the number line, far from where the vinegar had landed down low.

Grandma's face changed. "Wait. That soap is the same kind as the bar I use on my face. My sister keeps telling me it's too harsh, and I keep telling her to mind her own business." She paused, twisting the dust rag in her hands. "Could you test that one too?"

Brooklyn ran water over a sliver of the bar soap until it was cloudy, then dipped a fresh strip. Red to blue again, same spot on the chart. Grandma watched with her arms folded, and for a moment Brooklyn thought about the vinegar she'd tested at school two weeks ago, the one she'd labeled wrong. She had wanted to argue with Mr. Thompson about the grade. Now she was glad she hadn't, because he had been right, and being right mattered more when you could prove it.

"So it's true, then," Grandma said slowly. "I suppose I owe my sister a phone call. Maybe an amendment to the whole speech I gave her at Easter."

Brooklyn laughed, then inhaled the sharp clean smell of the soap as she sealed the strips in a labeled bag for Monday. She wrote "sink soap, base, 9 to 10" and underneath it, "face soap, same."

Grandma was already reaching for the phone on the wall. "Hello, Vivian? Don't say a word. Just don't say a word."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In the Sally-Anne test, first used in 1985, children from about age four usually say a character will look where she left her marble, not where it was moved while she was away.
story:
"Watch this," Anis whispered, pulling Violet toward the kitchen table where her little cousin was stacking plastic dinosaurs into a wobbly tower.

Violet had come over to work on their science homework, a poster about food chains, and the poster was still blank in her backpack. But the cousin, who had just turned three that month, was far more interesting than a poster. Could a kid that small remember where she put things? Could she guess what somebody else was thinking?

"She hides stuff constantly," Anis said. "Last week she buried my phone in the sock drawer."

"Then let's try something," Violet said. She picked up a red marble from the games shelf and rolled it across the table so the cousin saw it go into a blue cup. Then Anis called her into the hall to "look at the cat," which did not exist. While she was gone, Violet tipped the marble into a green bowl nearby and covered the blue cup with a napkin.

"Where will she look for her marble?" Anis asked when the cousin came scampering back.

"The green bowl, obviously. She saw us move it," Violet said. Anis shook his head slowly, like he was waiting for something. Hmm, Violet thought. Was she missing something? The cousin had been gone. She hadn't seen the switch at all.

"Where's my marble?" the cousin demanded, hands on hips. Then she marched straight to the blue cup, lifted the napkin, and frowned at the empty space. She checked under the napkin twice, as if the marble might be hiding from her. She never once glanced at the green bowl, even though it sat right there in plain view.

"You knew she'd do that?" Violet asked.

"My brother told me about it," Anis said. "It's called the Sally-Anne test, from 1985. Kids from about age four usually say a character will look where she left her marble, not where it got moved while she was away."

"So she's not dumb, she just... believes it's still in the cup," Violet said slowly, letting the idea digest. It was strange and a little wonderful. The cousin's brain held a true memory and a false belief at the same time, and the belief won. Did everyone walk around like that, certain of things that weren't so? Did Violet herself?

The cousin had started to wail about the vanished marble, so Violet slid the green bowl toward her. The marble gleamed there. The wail stopped instantly.

"Ta-da," Violet said.

"You're a carnivore with that marble," Anis joked, holding up a plastic T-rex. "Straight to the kill."

"A nutritious snack," Violet said, and the cousin solemnly fed the marble to the dinosaur, then looked up at Violet and asked, "More?"

"Okay, okay," Violet laughed, glancing at her backpack. The poster could wait. She grabbed the bag of marbles from the shelf and shook it. "Which one do you want to lose this time?"

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: The Northeast blackout that began on August 14, 2003, cut power to about 55 million people in parts of the northeastern United States and Ontario, Canada.
story:
Max stood at Ms. Kobayashi's front window while his mom finished filling the bathtub at home, just in case the water pumps failed too. Every house on the street was dark. He had a theory forming, and theories needed evidence.

"Maybe it's just our block," he said to Callum, who had come over with Juliette because Ms. Kobayashi had the biggest porch and the best cookies. "Or maybe just our street lost a fuse or something."

"Go look at the corner, then," Juliette said. "If the traffic light at Main is out, it's bigger than us."

Max borrowed the flashlight and walked to the corner in his sandals. The traffic light hung dead over an intersection with four cars treating it like a four-way stop. He looked north toward the mall and saw nothing but black where the parking lot lights should have been. Whatever the cause was, it was invisible and huge, and his small theory about a blown fuse had just failed its first test.

When he got back, Ms. Kobayashi's mother, who everyone called Gran even though she wasn't their grandmother, was sitting on the porch steps in the last orange light of the sky. "You look like someone who just proved himself wrong," she said.

"The whole grid's out," Max said. "Not just us."

Gran laughed. "There was a blackout on August 14, 2003, that cut power to about 55 million people, parts of the northeastern United States and Ontario, Canada. I walked home from work that whole way. Ten miles in my work shoes." She shook her head. "I remember deciding not to stop and call anyone. I wanted my own feet to get me home, and I've never decided if that was stubbornness or something better."

"Fifty-five million," Callum repeated. "That's like everyone in our state, times a lot."

Juliette was squatting by the compost bin at the side of the porch, shining her phone's dying screen into it. "Max, come look. I think someone's going to accuse you of throwing your banana peel in the wrong bin, because there's a whole pile of stuff that never should be in here." She held up a plastic wrapper. "The decomposers can't break this down, ever."

Gran peered over. "The bin's neutral ground tonight," she said. "Whatever's in it, nobody's in trouble."

Max sat down on the step beside Gran. He had another idea now, a small one he could actually test. He remembered that Ms. Kobayashi kept a battery radio in the kitchen drawer for emergencies, and he got up to find it, working the dial slowly through the static until a voice came through.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: A canoe is most stable when paddlers keep their weight low and centered, which is why people step into the middle of a canoe rather than onto its side.
story:
Cole stood at the end of the wooden dock with his duffel bag at his feet and a life jacket zipped up to his chin, because Mr. Cohen, whose cabin sat at the far side of the lake, had said the water was colder than it looked. Tomorrow morning the camp bus would pull out of the parking lot, and Cole would be on it, gone for six weeks. That part felt fine. The part that didn't feel fine was that he had never been in a canoe, and his cabin mate assignment sheet had said canoeing twice a week.

"You could just try it now," Petra said from the dock, her sandals dangling over the water. "Mr. Cohen said you could borrow his. It was practically a whole negotiation. I had to promise to water his tomatoes while he's visiting his sister." Jasper, sitting cross-legged beside her, was eating crackers and watching the way the waves made the light jump.

Cole looked at the green canoe tied at the dock's edge, rocking softly against the tire bumper. He stepped down onto the side of it, near the gunwale, and the canoe tipped so fast he grabbed the dock post with both hands. Water sloshed over the rim an inch from his sneakers.

"Whoa," Jasper said through a mouthful of cracker.

Cole knelt there, one foot on the canoe's edge, one hand white-knuckled on the post, and thought about it. It had tipped the moment his weight landed on the side. So the canoe didn't want weight high and out at the edge; it wanted weight low and in the middle. That was the whole trick, probably. He said it out loud, to prove it to himself: "You step into the middle. Keep low and centered." Petra raised an eyebrow, but she didn't argue.

He lowered himself slowly, both feet aimed at the center line, crouching like a crab, and the canoe barely swayed. When he finally sat down on the bottom, knees bent, the thing felt as steady as the dock. He found the paddle and pushed off, and the trees along the shore started to slide past. The water was so clear it seemed transparent all the way down to the rocks, but Petra had told him that was a lie lakes told; it only looked shallow. A fat bumblebee droned past his ear, heading for the purple flowers along the bank, doing its evening rounds to pollinate whatever it could before dark.

"You did it," Jasper called, standing up on the dock.

"Two weeks of tomatoes," Petra shouted after him, waving with both arms, though from out on the water she looked small, and Cole couldn't tell if she was waving goodbye to him for tonight or for the whole summer. He dug the paddle in and pulled, and the canoe swung toward the middle of the lake.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japanese homes, shoes are taken off in an entrance area called the genkan before stepping inside.
story:
The festival spread across the park beside the estuary, where the river widened and met the sea in flat brown water. Sarah had ten dollars in her pocket and one plan: find a birthday present for her grandmother before the booths closed at four. She had passed the scarf table and the pottery table twice without deciding, and now Avery was pulling her sleeve toward a new exhibit near the far fence.

"It's a Japanese house," Avery said. "Ayaan's family built it. You can go inside."

A line had formed at the doorway, where a raised floor marked the edge between the gravel path and the exhibit. Ayaan stood at the threshold in socks, and Sarah noticed a neat row of shoes lined up on the gravel, toes pointed outward, with a basket of slippers beside them. She was still wearing her sneakers.

"You have to take them off," Ayaan said to the family ahead of her. "This part is the genkan. Shoes come off here, before stepping inside."

Sarah worked through it as she waited. The whole exhibit was a rule made out of wood and gravel: the lower part by the door was for shoes, the raised part was for everything else, and nobody had to tell her twice because the row of shoes said it for them. She untied her sneakers, set them beside a pair of red rain boots, and stepped up in her socks.
