Inside, Ayaan's mother was pouring tea at a low table, and she pressed her palms together toward each guest with a small bow. Ayaan copied the gesture, then leaned toward Sarah and lowered his voice. "Watch. Some people pick up the cup with one hand. My grandmother would say to hold it with both hands." He wanted the visitors to do it right, Sarah could tell; he kept straightening the tea things after every group, and he winced when a man carried his cup across the tatami floor like a mug of coffee.

Sarah bought a small clay dish from the table near the door. "It's porous," Ayaan's mother said, turning it over. "Un-glazed on the bottom, so it should not hold water for long. For keys, or rings." It was three dollars, and Sarah thought of her grandmother's rings beside the kitchen sink, always sliding into the drain.

At the genkan on her way out, a girl from her grade stood frozen at the threshold, looking at the shoes and slippers, one sneaker already half off. "Am I supposed to..." she began.

"You take them off there," Sarah said, pointing at the gravel. "That part is the genkan. Shoes stay on the low side."

The girl kicked off both sneakers at once and scrambled up in her socks, and Ayaan caught Sarah's eye from the tea table and gave her a thumbs-up.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Many museums ask visitors not to touch objects, because oils and salts from skin build up over time and can stain or damage the surfaces.
story:
The fire station smelled like rubber boots and old coffee, and Evan had been looking forward to this field trip for two weeks. Station 9 was half museum, half working station, and their guide, a retired firefighter named Mr. Ong, had promised to show them everything from a hand-drawn pump cart from 1902 to the modern engines that could transport thousands of liters of water across town. Evan's real goal, though, was the firehouse dog, a solemn dalmatian named Chief who dozed near the watch desk where firefighters once logged every alarm by hand.

Mr. Ong unlocked the small room where the old records were kept, and the class crowded in around a heavy oak desk scarred with a century of use. Evan drifted toward it without thinking, fingers hovering over the wood, ready to run his hand along the edge the way he did with the banister at home.

"Whoa, stop." Emmett grabbed his sleeve. "You can't touch that. The oils and salts from your skin build up over time. It stains the wood. That's why everything in here has a rope in front of it, more or less."

Evan pulled his hand back and looked at the desk again, this time actually seeing it. The edges were dark and shiny where thousands of palms had rested, but the center of the writing surface was pale and dull. It was like a map of every hand that had ever worked there. He turned the idea over while Mr. Ong described how the alarm bell worked, and he began to notice the pattern everywhere: brass doorknobs gleaming gold, brass fixtures nobody touched gone brown and dusty. The damage wasn't sudden. It was gradual, invisible until you compared two surfaces.

He wanted to test it. On the walk to the apparatus bay, he kept his right hand in his pocket and let his left touch only things meant for touching: the rail of the viewing platform, the sample hose nozzle Mr. Ong passed around. When Moshe asked why he was walking like a penguin, Evan explained his experiment. "Every handrail in this station gets touched, right? And every desk and doorknob. I want to see if the pattern holds in the new part too, or if it's just the old stuff."

"Too many variables," Moshe said, shrugging. "New stuff hasn't had time."

"That's the point. Give it time and the same thing happens."

Mr. Ong overheard them and smiled. "Firefighters wipe the truck rails down every single day, you know." He nodded toward Engine 4, its chrome gleaming. "Not just for looks."

Evan felt his ears go warm. His rule still worked; somebody just interrupted the experiment on purpose. Then Mr. Ong pointed to the watch desk in the corner of the bay, a duplicate of the old one, used until fifteen years ago and never cleaned the same way. Its edges were already turning dark.

"See?" Evan whispered to Moshe. Moshe gave him a slow nod, impressed.

Then Chief the dalmatian trotted over, put one muddy paw directly on the old desk's pale center, and looked up at Evan as if daring him to say anything.

"Okay," Evan said, raising both hands, empty. "You win. Not touching."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Emergency agencies advise unplugging computers and other electronics during a power cut, because a surge of electricity when the power returns can damage them.
story:
The candles threw wobbling shadows up the living room wall, and Elliot sat on the rug with his phone at four percent battery, watching the screen like it might do something interesting. The whole street had gone dark at eight, right in the middle of his homework. "Unanimous vote," Grey had texted before the wifi died. "Movie night Friday, no exceptions." Now there was nothing to do but wait and listen to the refrigerator, which had stopped its usual humming for the first time in Elliot's whole life.

He got up and paced between the coffee table and the couch. Something was nagging at him, and it wasn't just boredom. He flashed back to two summers ago, when a storm had knocked the power out at his grandmother's house for a whole day. When it came back on, her desktop computer had made a sad clicking noise and never started again. She'd had to take it to a repair shop, and the repair guy had said one word to her that Elliot remembered now: "surge." When the power comes back, he'd told her, it can come back too hard for electronics, and it can damage them.

Elliot stood very still in the candlelight. The desktop computer in the corner, the one with all his school files on it, was still plugged in. So was the gaming console under the TV, and the TV itself. The power could come back any minute, and he pictured it rushing into the wall like water through a burst pipe. He grabbed a candle and carried it around the room, bending down to yank each plug out of its socket.

"What are you doing?" his little sister asked from the couch, where she'd been drawing houses by candlelight.

"Unplugging things. If the power comes back on and surges, it can damage the computer. Emergency agencies actually tell you to unplug electronics during a power cut." He tugged the console plug free and coiled the cord on the shelf. "Better safe than clicking noise forever."

His sister considered this. "Can I carry a candle?"

"You can hold my flashlight. My hands are full." She followed him around the room, shining the flashlight where he pointed, and the dark house felt less like a cave and more like a project. Nothing hindered them except the couch, which he barked his shin on, and which his sister found hilarious.

Later, when the lights blazed back on at half past nine, the hallway bulb flared and steadied. The unplugged computer sat silent and safe in its corner. Elliot plugged everything back in, and the desktop booted up exactly as it should. He flopped onto the couch beside his sister and texted Grey: "Power was out. Saved the computer. I'm basically an emergency agency." Then he picked up her flashlight, clicked it on and off twice, and handed it back.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, using peach baskets as the goals.
story:
The championship game went to a timeout with the score tied, and Luke's little brother's team huddled at the bench while the zamboni door stood open at the far end of the rink. Gwendolyn passed the popcorn down the row. Megane wasn't watching any of it. She had her phone out, thumb hovering over a trivia app that was giving away free skate passes to whoever cracked the weekly question.

"Who invented basketball?" Megane read. "I need this. I've wanted those passes since September, and I keep missing by one question." She typed a name fast, some actor, and the screen flashed red. "One guess left, and it's a team question, so help me."

Luke leaned over. He stared at the question, and his eyes drifted up to the wall behind the penalty box, where the rink had hung two old wooden peach baskets as decoration, the kind nobody ever asked about. Peach baskets. He had heard an anecdote about them somewhere, his grandfather going on about old sports at Thanksgiving, and one detail had stuck because it was such a strange picture: goals that were actual baskets, with the ball getting stuck and someone poking it out. If the goals were baskets, that was probably why it was called basketball, and if the game started with baskets, it had to be old, and old meant a gym somewhere, not a stadium.

"They were peach baskets," Luke said slowly. "The goals. That's why it's called a basket." He was building the rest of it in his head, the way he did with math proofs. "So think gyms. Training schools. Massachusetts, somewhere like Springfield." Gwendolyn said she'd heard the YMCA thrown around once. Megane typed: James Naismith, December 1891, YMCA training school, Springfield, Massachusetts, peach baskets as goals. The screen went green and the whole row of them whooped so loudly that a man two seats over shushed them, then ruined it by grinning.

The timeout ended and the game came back hard, and Luke's brother's team took a penalty that seemed to violate every rule of smart defense, giving up a power play with ninety seconds left. The other team scored on it. The rink went half desolate, the home fans slumping into their coats while a small knot of visitors celebrated at the far boards. Megane held up her phone showing the passes, three of them, and Gwendolyn asked which game they'd go see, since it wouldn't be this one.

Luke watched his brother skate off without looking up at the stands. "Maybe we save them," he said. "For when he wins something." Megane and Gwendolyn traded a look over his head, the kind that suggested they had already picked a Saturday, and Megane started scrolling through the app's next question. "This one's about hockey," she said. "You're going to want to hear this."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: Copying =SUM(B2:B10) one column to the right turns it into =SUM(C2:C10), because ordinary cell references are relative and shift with the formula.
story:
Emile sat cross-legged on Joyce's living room floor with her laptop between them, staring at a grid of numbers that refused to cooperate. The spreadsheet held three weeks of counts from their science project: animals their class had recorded on a wildlife camera pointed at a stretch of tundra habitat at the edge of the nature reserve. Lemmings, arctic foxes, one stubborn snowy owl that kept landing in front of the lens and blocking everything. Joyce had typed the counts in neat columns, one column per week, and now they needed totals.

"Mr. Chatterjee wants a bar chart by Monday," Emile said. "An objective chart, his word, not one that looks impressive but doesn't tell us anything." He clicked into the cell under the first column and typed =SUM(B2:B10). The total appeared, forty-three, and he sat back like he'd finished a marathon.

"That's one column," Joyce said. "We have three."

Emile groaned. He thought about last summer, when he'd spent an entire afternoon filling his grandfather's bird journal with tallies because he didn't know you could add a whole page at once. His grandfather had finally leaned over, drawn a single line through the numbers, and written one total. Emile had stared at it, feeling both silly and thrilled, and he'd promised himself he'd learn how to make things add themselves. He was not going to count forty-two cells by hand today.

He highlighted the cell with the formula and copied it. Then he clicked the cell one column to the right, under the second week, and pasted. The total that appeared was definitely not the total of column B. "Wait," he said slowly. He clicked the pasted cell, and there in the formula bar it read =SUM(C2:C10). He hadn't typed that. He had typed B, and the spreadsheet had changed it to C all by itself.

"Did it break?" Joyce asked, leaning in so close her face nearly magnified the screen reflection.

"It moved." Emile copied the formula again and pasted it one more column right, into the space under week three. =SUM(D2:D10). The numbers were different in every total, and he checked week two by hand, adding the column on paper, and it matched. The formula shifted when you copied it across. "They're relative," he said, mostly to himself. "The letters shift with the formula. So I copied one formula across the row and it totalled every column at once."

Joyce grabbed his arm. "Do the chart now. Highlight the totals and the week labels."

Emile selected the row of totals, clicked the chart button, and three bars climbed up the screen, week two clearly the tallest. He reached for the keyboard again. "What if we sort the animals too?"

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: Before fitting a new tube, the inside of the tyre should be checked for the thorn or glass that caused the flat, or it will puncture again.
story:
The driving school on Miller Road ran car lessons in the parking lot, but on Saturdays the back room belonged to the bicycle safety course, and that was where Anna found herself at nine in the morning with a flat tyre in her hands. Ms. Tehrani had wheeled out a rack of old bikes and set three on the floor with their wheels off. "Patch or replace, your choice," she said. "But every one of these went flat for a reason."

Anna had wanted this course since September, when she'd had to postpone joining because of her broken wrist, and now that the cast was off she wasn't going to waste a single minute. She picked the bike closest to her, slid a tyre lever under the edge of the tyre, and worked the bead loose the way the poster on the wall showed. Jessy knelt beside her, struggling with her own lever until it snapped out of her grip and clattered across the floor. Anna handed her the spare from the tray without being asked, and Jessy grinned.

The new tube went in smoothly. Anna tucked the valve through the rim, pressed the tyre back on with her thumbs, and pumped until the tube felt firm. Sean pumped his up too, and the three of them wheeled their bikes outside to the little practice loop behind the building, because Ms. Tehrani believed the final check should always be a real ride, however short.

Halfway around the loop, Anna's tyre went soft under her. She stopped, put a hand on the handlebar, and felt the wheel wobble against her palm. She stared at it, annoyed, and then a thought crept in. She hadn't looked inside the tyre. She'd been in a hurry, proud of her fast hands, and she'd never once run her fingers around the inside of the tyre to check for the thorn or the glass that caused the flat in the first place. If something sharp was still in there, it would puncture the new tube too. That would explain everything.

She wheeled the bike back inside, levered the tyre off again, and felt along the inside, careful and slow. Near the valve her fingertip caught on something small and hard. A splinter of glass, wedged deep in the rubber, waiting patiently to do its work a second time. She worked it out with the tip of a lever and held it up to the light. "Found it," she said. "You have to check the inside before you fit a new tube, or it just pops again." Sean looked down at his own freshly pumped wheel and didn't say anything.

Ms. Tehrani came over with the paperwork for the course settlement, the form that said who had completed which module, and her pen hovered over Anna's name. Then she looked at the glass splinter still lying in Anna's palm, and at Anna, and she signed nothing. "Ride the loop one more time," she said. Anna rolled the bike to the door and stopped, because her front tyre was going flat again, right there on the smooth concrete floor, where there was nothing sharp at all.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Acrylic paint is thinned with water while wet, but once it dries it becomes water-resistant, so brushes must be washed before the paint dries on them.
story:
Rose dragged the old picnic table across the backyard, her shirt already starting to perspire in the afternoon heat, and set down the wooden birdhouse she was painting for her grandmother's birthday. The plan was a mural of sunflowers, because Grandma had spent forty years in agriculture and claimed she could smell a field of them with her eyes closed. Rose wanted this to be the best thing she had ever made.

Then she opened the jar of brushes, and her stomach dropped. Every one of them stood stiff as a stick. She squeezed the bristles, and they didn't bend at all. Last night she remembered, in a quick flashback, standing at the sink with Mikhail, both of them laughing about something Alex had said at school, paint still glossy on the brushes, and her mother calling her in for dinner. "Tomorrow," she had told herself. Tomorrow had clearly won.

"Those are ruined," Mikhail said from the fence, peering over. He had come to see the sunflowers, and he was hoping Rose would let him paint the sky behind them, since he'd been sketching clouds all week and wanted proof he could do them for real. "My dad did that once with a whole set. He had to throw them out."

Rose frowned and turned one brush over in her hand. The paint had gone hard, like plastic. But yesterday the paint had been thin and smooth, and she remembered adding water to a dish of yellow and watching it spread out easily. So the paint was friendly to water when it was wet. It only turned stubborn later, once it dried. That meant the stiff bristles were dried paint, not a ruined brush. And if wet paint could be thinned with water, maybe more of the same paint would soften the old paint again. It was a guess, but it was a testable guess.

"Give me ten minutes," she said, and fetched a cup of warm soapy water. She swirled one brush in circles, pressing the bristles against the bottom of the cup. Nothing. She kept going, and then the tip began to flex, just slightly. She pressed harder, working the soap in, and a ribbon of orange paint clouded the water. The brush bent. It actually bent.

"Alex!" Mikhail yelled over the fence, because Alex had just appeared in the alley with a bag of chips. "Get over here, Rose fixed them!" Alex vaulted the fence, and Rose held up the brush, bristles gleaming and soft, then jabbed it toward the two of them like a tiny sword. "You do the sky," she told Mikhail, handing him a clean, fat brush. "And next time we wash them before dinner."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: At the same yearly rate, interest compounded monthly grows a little faster than interest compounded yearly, because each month's interest starts earning sooner.
story:
Emilia stood in line at the bank with her mother, holding the two brochures she had picked from the rack by the door. Both banks offered savings accounts at four percent a year, and both promised to keep that rate for five years. One said interest was compounded yearly, the other monthly, and as far as Emilia could tell, four percent was four percent. She was trying to conserve what she had earned from two summers of dog walking, three hundred and forty dollars, and she wanted it in the right place.

Kelsey had texted her that morning: "Just pick the one with the free tote bag." Emilia had not replied. The tote bag bank was the yearly one, and something about the fine print on the monthly one kept pulling at her. In the waiting area she took out a pencil and started an analysis on the back of the brochure, writing out what four percent a year meant, one year at a time, and then trying it month by month, smaller pieces but more of them.

Mr. Robinson, the neighbour who had first told her mother about these accounts, sat two chairs down waiting for a teller. He leaned over, saw her columns of numbers, and said nothing at first, which Emilia appreciated. The bank itself was quiet that afternoon, the carpet muffling footsteps, the pens chained to the desks, a clock ticking somewhere behind the roped-off counters.

Here was the twist. When she checked her math, the monthly account came out slightly ahead after five years, only a few dollars, but definitely ahead. She added it a second time, then a third, because two accounts at the same rate were supposed to end up equal, weren't they? Then she saw it. At the same yearly rate, interest compounded monthly grew a little faster than interest compounded yearly, because each month's interest started earning sooner. The monthly bank was not being generous and the yearly bank was not cheating; the timing itself made the difference. "It's the same four percent either way," she said to Mr. Robinson, mostly to herself. "But the monthly one gets a head start every single month."

"I believe you've got it," he said, and went back to his magazine, indifferent to the whole question now that she had settled it. When her mother's turn came, Emilia tugged her sleeve and held up the monthly brochure. "This one," she said, and slid the deposit slip across the counter toward the teller.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: The American Camp Association was founded in 1910, under the name Camp Directors Association of America, to set common standards for organized camps.
story:
The sign at the camp gate read American Camp Association Accredited, and Felix read it four times before the bus doors hissed shut behind him. First time at camp, first time more than two hours from home, first time carrying his own duffel up a gravel path that seemed determined to transform his sneakers into dust rags. He had exactly one plan: figure out what that sign meant before anyone figured out he was homesick.

"It's like a badge," said Veda, the girl who had claimed the bunk above his and already hung a string of paper cranes from the beam. "Camps collect badges. This one collects them about itself."

"A badge for what, though?" Felix set his duffel on the floor with a thud that made the cranes sway. "Nobody hangs a sign for nothing."

His cabinmate Bella shrugged from the doorway, where she was balancing a paddle like a tightrope walker. "Maybe it's a club. Secret handshake, weird hats, the works."

That night Felix lay awake doing what he did best, which was noticing patterns nobody asked him to notice. The counselors checked the lake ropes every single morning, even in pouring rain. The kitchen posted inspection sheets with actual signatures. Water drills happened so often the campers joked about them, and the jokes themselves felt rehearsed, like a phenomenon everyone had agreed to find funny. It all had to come from somewhere. Rules did not grow on trees, and camp directors were not famous for inventing paperwork for fun.

The next morning he tested his theory at the canoe dock, where Mr. Papadopoulos, the waterfront director, was coiling rope with enormous patience.

"Is the camp in trouble?" Felix asked. "Like, on probation?"

Mr. Papadopoulos laughed so hard he dropped the coil. "Probation? No, no. We passed. The sign means we meet the standards. They started in 1910, the Camp Directors Association of America, so organized camps would all follow common rules."

"Two thousand and twenty-four years of canoe checks," Felix said, mostly to himself.

"Something like that," said Mr. Papadopoulos, and pointed at the rope. "Grab that end."

By Thursday, Felix had turned it into a game, a cumulative scavenger hunt of standards: life jackets counted twice, the buddy board checked three times, one point awarded for every safety ritual spotted. Veda kept score on a napkin; Bella awarded bonus points for style. When the nurse taped a fresh first-aid sign inside the infirmary window, Veda shouted "Plus two!" so loudly that a chipmunk dove off the sill.

On Saturday morning Felix stood at the gate while waiting for the bus home, and he read the sign a fifth time. It looked different now, smaller and friendlier, like something you'd hang on a treehouse.

"Already scheming for next summer?" Veda bumped his shoulder with hers.

"Just checking the badge," Felix said. "Badges can expire."

"Not this one," said Bella, and she snapped a salute at the sign as the bus rolled in.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Many camps use a buddy system at the waterfront: each swimmer is paired with a partner, and at a 'buddy check' the pairs must find each other quickly so staff can count everyone.
story:
The canoe launch at Miller Pond had one wooden dock and a gravel beach, and Aaron arrived there early with a duffel bag full of cargo: two towels, a flashlight, and a stack of letters his mother had written in advance. Camp Kettleworth started in two days. Before he left, Ms. Flores had invited the three kids from the neighbourhood who had gone last summer to teach him the basics, so he would not look like a beginner on the first morning.

Arianne and Tara were already on the dock, dragging a green canoe into the shallows. "You steer from the back," Tara said, pointing at the stern seat. "Front person just paddles." They coordinated their strokes, and Aaron followed, chopping the water out of rhythm until Arianne called out, "Left, right, left," and the canoe finally ran straight.

They paddled to the far bank and back twice. On the second trip Arianne went quiet. She kept looking at the swimming area south of the launch, where orange floats marked off a rectangle of water, even though nobody was swimming there in the morning chill. When they beached the canoe, she stayed in the bow, dragging her paddle through the gravel.

"You okay?" Aaron asked.

"Fine," she said. "That's just the swim area."

Tara wiped her face with her sleeve and started rinsing the sand off her sandals, but she glanced at Arianne as she did it.

Aaron thought about that all through lunch on the dock. Arianne had said fine, but she had not stopped staring at the buoys. He tried out explanations. Maybe she hated swimming. Maybe something had happened on the water. But nothing in the story fit, because she had paddled the pond like she owned it.

He tested it directly. "Do you not like the water?" he asked.

"I love the water," Arianne said. "That's not it."

Tara folded her arms. "Just tell him. Otherwise he'll worry about it all week at camp."

Arianne pulled her paddle out of the gravel and laid it across her knees. "Last summer at Kettleworth, at swim time, I wandered off to the canteen. Just for fifteen minutes. I thought it was no big deal." She looked at the orange floats again. "My buddy was crying when I got back. Everybody got pulled out of the water."

Aaron waited, but that was all she said, and it made no sense to him. Why would a whole waterfront empty out because one person left? He turned it over while they loaded the canoe onto the rack. Then it landed. If every swimmer was paired with a partner, then one missing girl would mean one missing pair, and nobody could count heads properly. If the staff could not count, nobody could stay in the water. The whole system would break because of her.

"So they whistle, and everybody has to find their buddy fast," he said. "That's a buddy check. And yours couldn't find you, so they couldn't count anyone."

Arianne nodded. "They call it a buddy check," she said. "If you go, don't wander off during swim. Pick someone reliable."

"I'll be your buddy," Tara said. "You've learned your lesson, and I want my full swim time."

Arianne threw her paddle at her, and Tara caught it, laughing. Aaron hoisted his duffel, and they walked up the gravel road toward home, the orange floats still visible behind them, marking the empty water.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: USDA guidance says thawed freezer food can be safely refrozen if it still contains ice crystals or is at 40 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) or below.
story:
The lights died at 7:14 on a Tuesday, right in the middle of Sebastian's homework, and he let out a cheer so loud his dad yelled at him from the kitchen. "It's not a snow day," his dad called through the dark. "You still have math to finish." But Sebastian was already pulling on his boots, because when the power died at their house, it always died at the Hendersons' house too, and the Hendersons' neighbor, Mr. Hughes, had a generator, a porch light, and a standing invitation for the whole street.

"Power's out!" Sebastian announced on the porch, where Anika and Eddie were already sitting like they'd raced there. Eddie had beaten him by thirty seconds, which Eddie would never let him forget.

"Obviously," said Anika. "The question is what's happening to your freezer right now."

That was the problem that had been gnawing at Sebastian since the lights flickered. The freezer. Full of chicken, frozen pizzas, and three bags of peas, all slowly warming in the dark like a suspense movie. His family had thrown out everything after the last power cut, two whole garbage bags of food, and his mom had said something about it being hereditary bad luck with freezers, since her mother had done the exact same thing after a storm in 1996.

Mr. Hughes came out with a thermos of cocoa and a flashlight. "Last time it's out for four hours," he said. "Could be shorter. Could be you're sleeping on my porch."

"I need to verify something," Sebastian said, standing up. "If the food still has ice crystals when the power comes back, or if it's at forty degrees Fahrenheit, four degrees Celsius, or below, you can refreeze it. Safe. I read it on the USDA site for a science thing last year." He'd been waiting two years for this fact to be useful, and tonight was its moment.

"So your technique is what, exactly?" Eddie asked as they huddled under the porch light. "Stare really hard at your freezer from here?"

"Exactly," said Sebastian. "Staring technique. Very advanced."

At 9:40 the streetlights snapped back on and every kid on the porch cheered like their team had won a championship. Sebastian sprinted home, flung open the freezer, and grabbed the first bag of peas. It crunched. Actually crunched, hard little beads rattling inside, and when he squeezed one between his fingers he could feel the crystals, sharp and frozen under the plastic. He dug out the thermometer from the kitchen drawer, the one his mom used for candy making, and held it against a pizza box. Thirty-eight degrees.

"Mom!" he shouted up the stairs. "Mom, it's all still good! The peas have ice crystals and everything's under forty degrees Fahrenheit, four degrees Celsius! We can refreeze the whole thing!"

His mom came down in her pajamas and looked at the crinkled bag of peas, then at the thermometer, then at Sebastian, who was grinning so hard his face hurt.

"Well," she said, picking up the pizza and sliding it back into the freezer with ceremony, "the hereditary freezer curse ends tonight."

"Save the peas," Sebastian said. "They're the heroes."

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: In Mandarin Chinese, "Duōshǎo qián?" means "How much money?" and is the everyday way to ask a price.
story:
Nevaeh stood at the back of the line at the dumpling stall, mouthing the words Ms. Wiśniewski had drilled into them all week. Behind the folding table, steam rolled off the bamboo baskets, and the woman working the stall called out to each customer in Mandarin. Nevaeh's class had walked here from the language classroom for the field trip, and the deal was simple: order your food, ask the price, and get lunch. No English allowed.

Stefan was two people ahead of her, and he kept glancing back at the class like he wanted backup. He had wanted to be first in line all morning, because whoever ordered first got to pick the good table by the window, and he'd been telling everyone he'd claim it before Heath could. Now his confidence looked temporary. When he reached the front, he opened his mouth, and nothing came out. He pointed at the pork buns and held up one finger, then shuffled aside with his tray, having said nothing.

That was the problem, Nevaeh realized. The rule Ms. Wiśniewski had given them wasn't just about being polite. If you didn't ask the price, the woman had to guess what you wanted to know, and guessing slowed the line and frustrated everyone. Nevaeh tested her idea quietly while she waited: she listened to the man ahead of her, a regular customer, and heard him say a phrase she recognized. "Duōshǎo qián?" he asked, and the woman answered with a number.

That was it. That was the question from the flashcards. She'd been saying it wrong in her head all week, hitting the wrong tones, and hearing it from a real speaker fixed the sound in her memory. The pattern made sense now: you named the dish, then asked the question, and the answer came back as a price.

Heath leaned in behind her. "Just point like Stefan did."

"No," Nevaeh said. "I've got it."

She stepped up to the table. The steam warmed her face. She pointed at the vegetable dumplings and said the name carefully, then took the breath she'd been saving.

"Duōshǎo qián?"

The woman smiled, held up four fingers, and started filling a basket. Behind Nevaeh, Heath whispered to the kid after him, "Ask her how much. That's how it works."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Leave No Trace outdoor ethics are organized as seven principles, including 'dispose of waste properly' and 'leave what you find'.
story:
The trail above the river overlook was crowded with kids from Autumn's class, all of them on the eighth-grade spring trip to Pine Hollow National Park, and all of them pretending not to be as amazed as they were. Autumn crouched at the edge of the path, where a chunk of white quartz sat half buried in the dirt, glittering like it had a light inside it. Devin dropped down beside her and whistled.

"That's coming home with me," Devin said, working the rock loose. "My shelf has a spot that's been waiting for this."

"You can't just take things from a national park," Autumn said. Devin rolled his eyes in a way that meant he'd heard that before and had decided it didn't apply to him. That was the thing about Devin; he'd argue until sunset if you gave him the chance. But Autumn had noticed something earlier at the visitor center, a wooden sign near the bathrooms that she'd only half read while waiting in line. She was almost sure it had listed rules, and she was almost sure one of them had been about exactly this. Almost sure wasn't going to win the argument.

"Watch my brother's audition for the talent show tonight," Devin said, tucking the rock into his jacket. "Then tell me rules matter. He's been rehearsing a juggling act, and the fire alarm inspection is imminent, so the whole thing might get cut off anyway. Rules ruin everything."

Autumn jogged back down the path to the visitor center, dodging a man with a tripod, and found the sign again. It was titled Leave No Trace, and beneath the title it listed seven principles, each one printed in green letters. She ran her finger down them. Dispose of waste properly. Leave what you find. There it was, plain as a trail marker. Seven principles, and taking a pretty rock home broke one of them. She thought about the math of it: if four hundred kids a week each took one rock, the trail would slowly go bald, and no single kid would ever feel responsible. The cause was invisible, but she could add it up.

She found Devin near the overlook and pulled him aside, away from Harley, who was busy photographing a marmot. "It's called Leave No Trace," she said quietly. "Seven principles. One of them is leave what you find."

Devin looked at the river below, then at his jacket pocket, and his shoulders dropped. "It's just one rock."

"It's one rock four hundred times."

He pulled it out and turned it over in his palm. "Fine," he said, but he didn't sound bitter, exactly. He walked it back up the trail, knelt in the dirt, and pressed the quartz into its old hole, adjusting it until it sat level, the way it had before. Then he stood and dusted off his knees.

"Take a picture of it," he told Harley. "If my brother's act survives the fire alarm tonight, I'm showing him what leaving something behind looks like."

Harley raised the camera, and the shutter clicked just as the light caught the quartz, still shining.

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: A pivot table treats 'Gr 7' and 'Grade 7' as two separate groups, so answers must be typed consistently before they are summarised.
story:
Chase flopped onto Trystan's couch with his laptop balanced on a cushion. The school survey was due Monday, and Mr. Ahmed had said the summaries had to be "clean, clear, and actually correct," which felt like three separate insults aimed directly at Chase.

"Two hundred and six answers," Chase said. "Watch me make a pivot table do all the work." He dragged the Grade column into rows, dragged Votes into values, and grinned. Then the grin slid off his face. The table listed Grade 6, then Gr 7, then Grade 7, then Grade 8.

"Your spreadsheet has twins," Trystan said, leaning over with a granola bar in one hand.

"There should be four grades, not five." Chase squinted at the numbers. Gr 7 had forty-one votes. Grade 7 had forty-three. He scrolled through the raw answers, and there it was: some students had typed "Gr 7" and others had typed "Grade 7," depending on whether they were in a hurry or just liked typing more letters. The pivot table had no idea they were the same thing. He drummed his fingers. "So every vote is real, they're just split between two labels."

"What are you going to do, yell at everyone's keyboards?" Trystan offered him half the granola bar, which was his way of saying he had no ideas but plenty of sympathy.

Chase copied the data to a safe sheet first, so he could retrieve the original if everything exploded. Then he tried an idea. He sorted the Grade column, found every "Gr 7," and changed them all to "Grade 7," checking twice that nothing else got touched. Consistent labels, he figured, were the whole game; the camouflage had fooled the machine, not him. He rebuilt the pivot table.

Grade 7 appeared once, with all eighty-four votes. Grade 6 had fifty-nine, Grade 8 had sixty-three, the same totals as before, only finally together where they belonged. Chase raised both fists like he'd scored in overtime.

Trystan peered at the screen, chewing. "So it was hiding in plain sight the whole time."

"Basically a spreadsheet wearing camouflage." Chase hit save three times, which was two more than necessary, and started typing the summary for Mr. Ahmed.

From the doorway, Trystan's mom called that pizza was on its way, and Chase said, "Perfect. Grade seven demands dinner."
